title: Accounting Services in Bali: Monthly Deliverables
contentHtml:
Accounting services bali monthly deliverables should be more than a spreadsheet of transactions. A useful monthly engagement should produce reconciled bank and booking records, properly supported income and costs, a clear profit-and-loss view, cash movement information, an exceptions list and an organised file of evidence. It should also explain what remains unresolved, distinguish bookkeeping from tax or legal advice, and make the next review easier for the owner, manager and authorised adviser.

For a Bali villa, the monthly close is a controlled handover: operational records become financial information that someone can understand, question and use. The exact scope depends on the entity, number of properties, transaction volume, accounting system and records supplied. Those boundaries should be written into the engagement before work begins.

Who this applies to

This guide is for owners and operators who are comparing monthly accounting providers or reviewing an existing engagement. It is particularly relevant to:

  • Foreign owners receiving booking payouts or management statements from Bali villas.
  • PT PMA companies that need property-level records, owner funding trails and organised files for professional review.
  • Villa managers handling supplier invoices, staff-related records, guest income and owner reporting.
  • Owners with more than one villa, shared suppliers or costs that need allocation.
  • Businesses moving from informal spreadsheets to a repeatable monthly close.

It is not a promise that every engagement includes every item below. A provider may reasonably separate bookkeeping, management reporting, tax compliance, payroll execution, company administration and advisory work. Ask which deliverables are included, which depend on records arriving on time and which require a separate engagement.

What a monthly engagement should deliver

1. A complete record-collection process

The month should begin with a defined request for records, not an open-ended message asking whether anything is missing. The request may cover bank statements, payment-platform reports, direct booking schedules, manager statements, supplier invoices, receipts, payroll-related source records, utility bills, loan or financing movements, owner payments and property-specific spending.

A good process identifies the reporting period, the person responsible for each source and the expected format. It also records documents not received. That missing-document log is important: an account may appear balanced while still lacking evidence for a material transaction.

For a practical model, see the Bali villa month-end close record-collection workflow. The goal is not to create paperwork for its own sake. It is to make the final numbers traceable to source documents.

2. Bank and cash reconciliation

Each relevant bank account should be compared with the accounting ledger for the same period. The reconciliation should identify outstanding deposits, payments recorded in the books but not yet cleared, bank charges, transfers between accounts and transactions that cannot yet be classified. Cash held by a manager or paid directly for property expenses may require a separate supporting schedule.

A reconciliation is not simply a statement that the bank balance “looks right”. It should show the closing statement balance, ledger balance and reconciling items. Old unreconciled entries should be carried forward with an explanation or investigated, rather than silently left in the system.

3. Booking and management-statement reconciliation

Booking value, guest charges, platform fees, refunds, taxes shown by a platform, management deductions and bank receipts are different figures. A monthly close should connect them. The provider should be able to explain why a booking report does not equal the amount deposited into the bank.

This is especially important where a manager collects funds before remitting an owner share. The report should distinguish gross booking activity, deductions and the net transfer. It should not label the bank receipt as the whole economic value of the booking without examining the supporting statement. The guide to reading a villa management statement provides a useful review framework.

4. Coded expenses with supporting evidence

Invoices and receipts should be attached or indexed to the relevant transaction where practicable. Costs should be coded consistently, such as utilities, cleaning, repairs, supplies, management fees, professional fees, property improvements and owner-related movements. A chart of accounts should be detailed enough to answer management questions without becoming so complicated that coding becomes inconsistent.

Shared expenses need an allocation method. For example, a bill serving two villas might be split using a documented basis agreed with the owner or manager. The method should be applied consistently and reviewed when circumstances change. An unexplained “general expense” line may be convenient, but it weakens property-level reporting.

5. Owner funding, withdrawals and reimbursements

Money paid into a business by an owner is not automatically revenue, and money taken out is not automatically an operating expense. The monthly pack should identify owner advances, capital contributions, loans where documented, reimbursements, personal payments and distributions or withdrawals according to the entity’s records and professional advice.

Each item should have a date, amount, account, description and supporting evidence. Where the accounting treatment depends on company documents or tax advice, the bookkeeper should flag the question rather than make an unsupported assumption. This protects the distinction between recording a transaction and deciding its legal or tax treatment.

6. A monthly reporting pack

At minimum, many villa owners need a profit-and-loss report, balance-sheet or position report where relevant, bank reconciliation summary, booking-income bridge, cash movement summary and open-items list. A multi-property owner may also need a property-by-property view and a consolidated view.

The report should explain significant movements from the previous month or from an agreed budget. A large change may result from seasonality, a delayed payout, a major repair, a one-off owner payment or incomplete records. Variance commentary should identify the reason known from the evidence and mark matters requiring confirmation.

For a broader reporting structure, compare the monthly villa management reporting pack. A report becomes useful when it helps an owner decide what to investigate, reserve, approve or discuss with an adviser.

A useful monthly deliverables table

Illustrative monthly close deliverables for a Bali villa
DeliverableEvidence reviewedUseful output
Bank reconciliationBank statements, ledger and transfer recordsReconciled balance and outstanding items
Booking reconciliationReservation, platform, manager and payout reportsGross-to-net booking bridge
Expense reviewInvoices, receipts and approval notesCoded expense schedule and missing evidence list
Owner activity reviewBank entries, payment descriptions and supporting documentsFunding, reimbursement and withdrawal schedule
Property allocationSupplier bills and agreed allocation basisProperty-level cost report
Management reportingClosed ledger and prior-period informationP&L, cash summary and variance notes
Open-items registerUnresolved transactions and late documentsNamed questions, owner and next action

The table is a scope conversation, not a mandatory package. Some businesses need fewer reports; others need more frequent transaction processing or a separate management-accounting service. The important point is that the deliverables are specific enough for both parties to recognise completion.

Worked IDR example: tracing a month correctly

The following is an illustrative bookkeeping example only. It is not a tax calculation. Assume a villa’s reservation and payout records for one month show booking charges of IDR 48,000,000. The manager deducts a management fee of IDR 7,200,000 and approved operating purchases of IDR 4,800,000 before transferring the balance.

The arithmetic is:

  • Booking charges: IDR 48,000,000
  • Less management fee: IDR 7,200,000
  • Less approved operating purchases: IDR 4,800,000
  • Expected transfer: IDR 48,000,000 − IDR 7,200,000 − IDR 4,800,000 = IDR 36,000,000

Suppose the bank statement shows IDR 35,500,000 received. The unexplained difference is IDR 36,000,000 − IDR 35,500,000 = IDR 500,000. The monthly close should not force the bank receipt to match the expected transfer. It should place IDR 500,000 in the exceptions register and ask whether there was a bank charge, additional deduction, timing difference, refund or recording error.

If the manager’s statement separately shows a bank charge of IDR 500,000, the bridge can be completed: IDR 48,000,000 − IDR 7,200,000 − IDR 4,800,000 − IDR 500,000 = IDR 35,500,000. That explains the bank receipt. Whether each item receives a particular tax or accounting treatment depends on the responsible professional and the underlying facts; the bookkeeping task is to preserve the trail and present the distinction clearly.

What owners get wrong

1. “The bank balance is enough.”

Correction: The bank shows cash movement, not necessarily the full booking activity, unpaid supplier obligations, owner funding or costs withheld by a manager. Require reconciliations that connect bank receipts to booking and management reports.

2. “A monthly fee means everything is included.”

Correction: Ask for an engagement scope. Preparation of records may be included while tax advice, tax registration, compliance submissions, payroll execution, audit support, company changes or visa administration require separate work. Submission work should be performed by the responsible authorised person under a separate engagement, not assumed to be part of ordinary monthly bookkeeping.

3. “Unresolved items can be fixed at year-end.”

Correction: Require an exceptions register every month. A missing invoice, unclear owner payment or unexplained payout difference is easier to resolve while the manager, bank record and transaction context are still accessible.

Questions to put in the engagement letter

Before appointing a provider, ask precise questions rather than relying on labels such as “full accounting”.

  • Which bank, platform, manager and payment accounts are included?
  • How many properties, entities and monthly transactions does the fee cover?
  • Are booking reconciliations prepared from reservation-level data or only payout totals?
  • How are shared costs, owner payments and property improvements identified?
  • What reports are issued, in what format and at what point in the monthly cycle?
  • Does the pack include an exceptions register and missing-document log?
  • Who reviews unusual transactions and who approves final classifications?
  • Which tax, payroll, licensing, company-formation or compliance services are excluded?
  • What happens when records arrive late or are incomplete?
  • How are files handed over if the owner changes provider?

A provider’s answer should describe a process, not just a result. If the owner cannot see how evidence moves from collection to reconciliation to reporting, the engagement may be difficult to supervise.

Printable monthly close checklist

Use this checklist as a discussion tool with the person responsible for the records. Tick each item only when it is complete or formally listed as unresolved.

  1. Confirm the reporting period, entity and properties included.
  2. Collect bank statements for every relevant account.
  3. Collect OTA, direct-booking and villa-manager reports.
  4. Match booking activity to deductions, refunds and transfers.
  5. Record missing reports and documents in the exceptions register.
  6. Reconcile each bank account to the ledger.
  7. Review supplier invoices, receipts and approval evidence.
  8. Separate repairs, supplies, improvements and owner-related payments.
  9. Apply the documented method for shared-cost allocation.
  10. Identify owner advances, reimbursements, withdrawals and transfers.
  11. Review unusual or high-value transactions with the responsible owner.
  12. Prepare the profit-and-loss and cash movement reports.
  13. Compare major movements with the previous period and add evidence-based notes.
  14. List every unresolved item with an owner and next action.
  15. Save the final reports, reconciliations and supporting index in an organised folder.
  16. Confirm whether any matter needs separate review by an authorised tax, legal or other professional.

For owners seeking a defined scope, Bali Accounting’s accounting and bookkeeping services can be discussed against the property structure, reporting needs and available records. A Client Advisory conversation through get started should establish what is included before any engagement is accepted.

This article provides general information about bookkeeping and reporting processes. It is not tax, legal, immigration, licensing or financial advice, and it does not state current rates, thresholds, deadlines or filing obligations. General articles are not individual advice or evidence of professional review. Treatment and any submission work require the responsible authorised person and a separate engagement where applicable.

Frequently asked questions

What should I receive from monthly accounting services in Bali?

You should expect clearly defined outputs such as reconciled bank records, booking or management-statement reconciliation, coded expenses, owner-activity schedules, management reports and an exceptions list. The exact package depends on the engagement and the records supplied.

Is a profit-and-loss report enough for a Bali villa?

Usually not. A profit-and-loss report explains recorded income and expenses, but it does not by itself explain cash balances, booking deductions, owner funding, unpaid costs or unresolved evidence. A useful monthly pack connects these areas.

Should the bookkeeper decide how an owner payment is treated?

The bookkeeper can record the transaction and identify the evidence, but classification may depend on company documents, accounting policy or professional tax advice. Uncertain items should be flagged for the responsible authorised adviser rather than guessed.

Are tax filings included in a monthly bookkeeping engagement?

Not automatically. Filing, tax compliance, tax registration and tax advice should be stated separately in the engagement. Preparation and submission work require the responsible authorised person and may require a separate scope.

What if my villa manager does not provide a complete statement?

Record the missing information in an exceptions log, retain the available bank and booking evidence, and ask the manager for the specific missing fields. Do not present an unexplained payout as fully reconciled merely because cash arrived.

How often should owners review the monthly pack?

Review it after the close while transactions and operational context are still fresh. Focus on unexplained differences, major variances, owner movements, upcoming commitments and items that need an authorised adviser’s attention.

title: Airbnb Bookkeeping: Refunds, Cancellations and Payout Reserves
contentHtml:
Airbnb bookkeeping refunds cancellations reserves should be handled as separate record categories, not as one unexplained reduction in bank receipts. Start with the original reservation, identify the cancellation or refund event, record any platform adjustment, and reconcile the final payout to the bank. A reserve is different again: it is money retained or set aside for a known future obligation, not a refund and not automatically an expense.

For a Bali villa, this distinction matters because a monthly bank statement only shows settlement activity. It does not explain the booking value, guest refund, Airbnb service fee, manager deduction, delayed payout or cash retained for repairs. Good bookkeeping creates that explanation before an owner, manager or authorised adviser needs it.

Who this applies to

This guide is for owners, operators and management companies handling Airbnb reservations for one or more Bali villas. It is relevant whether the property is owned personally, through a company or under another arrangement, because the bookkeeping questions remain practical:

  • What did the guest reservation originally show?
  • What changed after a cancellation, alteration or refund?
  • What amount did Airbnb actually settle?
  • Which deductions were made by Airbnb or the manager?
  • Was money received, held, transferred or reserved?
  • Can every accounting entry be traced to a report, statement or approval?

The legal and tax treatment can vary according to the owner, entity, contract, payment flow and transaction classification. This article therefore focuses on evidence and reconciliation. It does not determine tax treatment, deductible expenses, reporting obligations or the correct treatment for a particular owner.

Why refunds and cancellations create bookkeeping problems

Airbnb records may contain several dates for one reservation: booking date, check-in date, cancellation date, refund date, payout date and bank settlement date. These dates answer different questions. If a bookkeeper posts every bank receipt as rental income, the accounts may omit the original booking value, conceal refunds or place activity in the wrong month.

A cancellation can occur before any payout, after a payout or after the guest has stayed for part of the reservation. A refund may be full, partial or connected to a reservation alteration. Airbnb may also adjust its own service fee, reverse an earlier transaction or combine several reservation adjustments in one settlement report.

For that reason, use a reservation-level reconciliation rather than relying on a bank-feed description. The reconciliation should connect the reservation reference to:

  1. the original guest charge or booking report;
  2. any cleaning fee, extra guest charge or other separately displayed component;
  3. Airbnb service fees and other platform deductions;
  4. the cancellation, alteration or refund record;
  5. the resulting payout or clawback;
  6. the bank receipt or payment leaving the account; and
  7. the explanation for any amount still pending.

Owners can read more about the wider process in Bali Airbnb bookkeeping and payout reconciliation. That workflow is useful because it treats the platform report and bank statement as connected but different records.

A practical classification framework

Use a consistent set of columns or accounts for each reservation. The names can be adapted to the chart of accounts, but the underlying distinctions should remain visible.

Suggested reservation and settlement records
Record areaWhat it explainsEvidence to retain
Original reservationThe guest-facing booking value before later changesReservation statement or platform report
Refund or cancellationThe amount returned, waived or reversedRefund notice, cancellation detail and approval where relevant
Platform feesAmounts withheld by Airbnb from settlementDetailed payout statement
Manager deductionsManagement fees, expenses or transfers taken outside AirbnbManagement statement and invoices
Bank settlementThe amount actually received or paidBank statement and payment reference
Payout reserveCash retained or earmarked for a future purposeReserve policy, transfer record and later use

The table is a bookkeeping map, not a tax conclusion. For example, a cleaning fee may be displayed separately by the platform but still require review against the underlying service arrangement. A manager deduction may be an operating charge, an owner payment or a pass-through amount depending on the contract and evidence. Do not decide from the label alone.

Refunds

Record a refund against the reservation that generated it. If the refund is partial, preserve the original amount and show the reduction separately, rather than overwriting the booking record. This makes it possible to answer whether the villa earned less because of a guest concession, a cancellation policy, a service failure or a platform decision.

When a refund is paid directly from the platform, the bank may show only a lower net payout. When it is charged after an earlier payout, the bank may show a separate debit or a negative settlement. Both situations need a link to the same reservation reference.

Cancellations

A cancellation is an event; the financial result depends on what was retained, returned or reversed. Keep the cancellation date and reason visible, but do not assume that a cancelled reservation has no financial effect. A cancellation may produce a retained amount, a partial refund, a full refund, a rebooking adjustment or no settlement at all.

If the platform report groups several cancellations into one payout adjustment, use a reconciliation schedule listing each reservation. The total of the schedule should agree to the grouped platform amount. An unexplained “cancellation adjustment” is not a sufficient audit trail.

Payout reserves

A reserve is a control over cash, not a description of revenue. It may refer to money retained by a platform, held by a manager or moved by the owner into a separate bank account for maintenance, refunds or another planned need. The records should state who controls the money, why it is being held, how it can be released and whether it remains part of the villa’s cash balance.

Do not reduce rental income merely because cash was transferred into a reserve account. Do not record a reserve as an expense merely because the owner intends to spend it later. The later payment needs its own supporting invoice, approval and classification.

Worked IDR example: one reservation through settlement

The following is an illustrative bookkeeping example only. It is not a tax calculation and does not assume any particular Airbnb contract, fee structure or regulatory treatment.

A villa reservation shows an accommodation charge of IDR 12,000,000 and a separately displayed cleaning charge of IDR 1,000,000. The guest later receives a partial refund of IDR 2,000,000. Airbnb withholds a platform fee of IDR 1,100,000. The manager then deducts an approved maintenance payment of IDR 900,000 before transferring the balance to the owner’s operating account.

The arithmetic is:

  • Original platform total: IDR 12,000,000 + IDR 1,000,000 = IDR 13,000,000.
  • Less guest refund: IDR 13,000,000 − IDR 2,000,000 = IDR 11,000,000.
  • Less Airbnb platform fee: IDR 11,000,000 − IDR 1,100,000 = IDR 9,900,000.
  • Less approved maintenance deduction: IDR 9,900,000 − IDR 900,000 = IDR 9,000,000.
  • Expected bank transfer: IDR 9,000,000.

The reconciliation should show IDR 13,000,000 as the original platform total, IDR 2,000,000 as the refund, IDR 1,100,000 as the platform deduction, IDR 900,000 as the supported maintenance payment and IDR 9,000,000 as the final transfer. The bank receipt alone would not explain those components.

Suppose the owner then moves IDR 2,000,000 from the operating account into a separately labelled maintenance reserve. The cash movement is:

  • Bank transfer received: IDR 9,000,000.
  • Less transfer to maintenance reserve: IDR 2,000,000.
  • Operating account balance increase from this reservation: IDR 7,000,000.
  • Maintenance reserve balance increase: IDR 2,000,000.

The IDR 2,000,000 reserve transfer is not another refund and is not the IDR 900,000 maintenance deduction. They are different events with different evidence. Later, when a supplier invoice is paid from the reserve, record that payment against the invoice and show the transfer between accounts if needed.

What owners get wrong

1. Treating the net bank payout as the booking revenue

Correction: retain the gross reservation components, refunds and platform deductions in the reconciliation. The bank amount is a settlement result, not necessarily the complete booking record. This approach also makes it easier to compare Airbnb activity with direct bookings and other OTAs.

2. Deleting cancelled reservations from the records

Correction: keep the original reservation reference and mark the financial outcome. A cancelled booking with no payout still supports occupancy analysis and explains why an expected receipt is absent. A cancelled booking with a retained amount or refund needs even more detail, not less.

3. Calling every retained balance an expense or profit

Correction: identify whether the amount is a platform hold, manager balance, owner transfer or reserve account movement. Then follow the cash and obtain evidence for the later release or payment. A reserve policy should specify purpose, approver, account and review date.

Monthly close process and printable checklist

Use the following as a practical month-end checklist. It can be printed or copied into an internal close file.

  1. Collect: download Airbnb reservation, transaction and payout reports for the month, including reports covering earlier reservations adjusted during the month.
  2. Identify: list new bookings, cancellations, partial refunds, full refunds, reservation alterations, negative payouts and pending settlements.
  3. Match: connect each platform transaction to a reservation code and, where applicable, to a manager statement or supplier invoice.
  4. Recalculate: for each payout group, add reservation amounts and subtract refunds and platform deductions to reach the reported settlement.
  5. Agree: compare reported settlements with bank receipts and record timing differences separately.
  6. Review: investigate duplicated refunds, missing payout lines, unexpected negative balances and deductions without invoices.
  7. Separate: classify operating costs, owner withdrawals, transfers between bank accounts and reserve movements distinctly.
  8. Document: save the report, bank evidence, approval and explanation together using a consistent file name.
  9. Escalate: prepare questions for the responsible accounting or tax adviser when ownership, contracts, related parties or treatment is unclear.
  10. Close: list unresolved items, their owner, expected evidence and the period in which the issue should be revisited.

A useful close pack should include a payout reconciliation, refund and cancellation schedule, reserve movement summary, bank reconciliation and open-items list. It should also show whether a manager has withheld funds that have not yet reached the villa account.

For owners with several villas, keep the property identifier on every reservation and deduction. Shared management charges should not be allocated by guesswork. Use the documented basis agreed for the business and retain the supporting calculation. The guide to shared-cost allocation for Bali rental properties provides a related record-keeping framework.

Controls for managers and owners

Refunds are particularly sensitive because the person approving a guest concession may not be the person reconciling the bank. Establish a simple separation of duties: the manager records the operational reason, an authorised person approves material exceptions, and the bookkeeper matches the platform and bank evidence.

Set a regular review for outstanding reserves. The review should answer how much is held, where it is held, what it is for, whether it relates to one villa or several, and whether any amount has remained unexplained for too long. A reserve without an owner, purpose or release history becomes a suspense balance.

Use the villa’s chart of accounts consistently. Refunds may require a contra-income or adjustment presentation in management reporting, while a platform fee, maintenance payment and owner withdrawal may belong in different sections. The correct presentation depends on the reporting purpose and adviser guidance. The important control is that the underlying transaction remains traceable.

If your current records combine Airbnb reports, manager statements and bank exports without reservation references, a scoped review can help identify missing links. Bali Accounting provides Airbnb bookkeeping for Bali villas, with preparation and any submission work handled only under a separate engagement by the responsible authorised person. For Client Advisory language about your records and reporting scope, use the Client Advisory enquiry page.

Records to prepare for an adviser

Before asking an authorised tax or legal adviser about treatment, assemble the evidence rather than sending only a bank statement. Useful records include the Airbnb host account reports, reservation history, cancellation and refund notices, payout details, management agreements, invoices, bank statements, reserve transfers, ownership documents and any written approval policy.

Also prepare a short issue list. Examples include: whether a separately displayed guest charge belongs in the same reporting category; whether a manager deduction is a cost or a pass-through; how a negative payout should be presented; and whether a reserve belongs to the villa, the company or the owner. These are questions for the appropriately licensed adviser, supported by a clean reconciliation.

For broader monthly controls, see the Bali villa bookkeeping checklist and the guide to reading a villa management statement. General information in this article is not tax, legal, accounting or financial advice for an individual situation. It is not evidence of professional review. Tax treatment, filing decisions and any submission require the responsible authorised person and a separate engagement; they are not automatic inclusions in monthly bookkeeping.

Image credit: Bali Accounting’s publisher-selected open-license image library. The illustrative image does not depict a client, client property or client records.

Frequently asked questions

Should a cancelled Airbnb booking remain in the books?

Yes. Keep the reservation reference and record the cancellation outcome, even where no money was received. This preserves the occupancy trail and explains missing or reversed expected payouts.

Is a refund the same as an Airbnb platform fee?

No. A refund changes the amount returned to the guest, while a platform fee is a charge or deduction associated with the platform service. They should be separately identified and supported by the relevant platform report.

How should an Airbnb payout reserve be recorded?

First identify who holds the money and why. A transfer into a separate reserve account is generally a cash movement in the bookkeeping records, not automatically an expense. The later payment needs its own evidence and classification.

What if Airbnb combines several refunds into one adjustment?

Prepare a schedule listing each reservation, refund amount and adjustment date, then reconcile the schedule total to the combined platform adjustment. Do not leave the grouped amount without reservation-level support.

Can this process determine my Bali tax treatment?

No. It helps organise evidence and reconcile transactions. The treatment of rental income, refunds, fees, reserves and ownership arrangements should be confirmed with the responsible authorised Indonesian adviser for the specific facts.

title: Rental Property Bookkeeping: Owner Contributions
contentHtml:
Owner contributions should be recorded separately from rental income. In rental property bookkeeping, a transfer from an owner is normally tracked as an owner funding or equity-related movement, while guest payments belong in the rental-income records. The distinction helps a Bali villa owner see operating performance, available cash, outstanding funding and reimbursements without treating every bank receipt as revenue.

Why the distinction matters

A villa can receive several kinds of money in the same month: booking payouts, direct guest deposits, a transfer from an owner to pay a contractor, a reimbursement for a personal payment, or funds held for a future renovation. They may all appear on one bank statement, but they answer different accounting questions.

Rental income explains what the property earned from accommodation or related services during the relevant accounting period. Owner contributions explain money introduced by an owner or related party to support the property or entity. An owner reimbursement records money returned to someone who paid a business cost personally. A loan or advance may create a liability rather than an owner-equity balance. The correct classification depends on the facts, documents and legal relationship.

If these movements are combined, a monthly report can show inflated revenue, understated funding, unclear profitability or an unexplained cash balance. That can make it harder to compare periods, assess whether the property is self-funding, answer questions from a qualified adviser, or hand over records to another bookkeeper.

This is a bookkeeping framework, not a conclusion about Indonesian tax treatment. Classification for tax, company law, related-party reporting or financial statements should be confirmed with the responsible authorised adviser.

Who this applies to

  • Owners of a Bali villa rented through online travel agencies, direct bookings or a management company.
  • Foreign owners using an Indonesian company, including a PT PMA, where company and personal funds must be distinguished.
  • Property managers who receive owner advances or pay expenses on an owner’s behalf.
  • Owners with more than one villa, especially where one bank account or team pays costs across several properties.
  • Bookkeepers preparing monthly reports that need to explain profit, cash and funding separately.

Build clear transaction categories

A practical chart of accounts should give each recurring movement a home. The exact account names can vary, but the meaning should remain consistent from month to month.

Illustrative categories for owner and rental-property movements
TransactionRecord asEvidence to retainWhy it matters
Guest booking payoutRental income, with platform deductions reconciled separatelyReservation report, payout statement and bank receiptShows the property’s operating revenue and explains the cash received
Owner transfers funds to the business accountOwner contribution, loan or advance pending documented classificationBank transfer, funding note and approvalPrevents funding from inflating rental revenue
Owner pays a villa supplier personallyExpense plus payable to owner, or contribution if formally treated that waySupplier invoice, payment proof and reimbursement requestConnects the cost to the villa and the person who funded it
Business repays the ownerOwner reimbursement or settlement of an owner balanceApproved claim and bank paymentShows cash leaving without recording a second operating expense
Funds set aside for a future projectSeparate reserve or funding balance according to the reporting policyOwner instruction, project estimate and transfer recordHelps distinguish restricted purpose funds from normal operating cash
Owner takes money from the businessOwner withdrawal, distribution or other documented movementApproval, bank proof and relevant agreementPrevents withdrawals being mistaken for property expenses

The word “contribution” should not become a catch-all. If an owner says, “I put money in,” the bookkeeping file should still ask what the money was intended to do, who legally received it, whether repayment is expected, and which property benefited. Where the answer is uncertain, use a clearly labelled suspense or review balance temporarily and resolve it through documentation rather than guessing.

For a broader process, compare this approach with PT PMA owner funding records in Bali. For personal and business separation, see how to fix mixed personal and villa money.

A monthly workflow for owner contributions

1. Collect the source records

Start with the complete bank statement, booking and platform reports, management statements, supplier invoices, payment approvals, owner transfer confirmations and reimbursement claims. Do not rely on a bank description alone. A transfer labelled “villa” does not prove whether it was income, funding, a loan, a reimbursement or a transfer between properties.

2. Match incoming funds to their source

For each receipt, identify the payer, purpose, related property, booking or project reference, and supporting document. Match platform receipts to reservation-level or payout-level reports. If a management company deducts fees before transferring the balance, retain the gross booking report and the deduction detail so the cash receipt can be traced without losing the underlying transaction.

The Bali villa OTA payout reconciliation workflow provides a useful companion process for connecting reservations, fees, refunds, transfers and bank receipts.

3. Record the owner movement separately

Use a consistent owner account for each owner or related party where practical. Record the date, amount, currency, receiving account, stated purpose, property and whether repayment is expected. If the transfer covers several properties, allocate it using an approved method and retain the allocation schedule.

4. Match expenses to the funding source and property

An owner contribution does not automatically become an expense. The expense is recorded when the villa receives goods or services and the supporting invoice is available. The funding entry explains how the cash was provided. Keeping both records allows a report to show the operating cost and the source of payment without duplicating either one.

5. Reconcile closing balances

At month end, compare the bookkeeping balance for each owner funding account with the transfers, approved reimbursements and withdrawals. Investigate unexplained differences. A short reconciliation note should explain opening balance, additions, settlements, closing balance and outstanding documents.

Illustrative IDR worked example

The following is an accounting illustration only. It is not a tax calculation and does not rely on any assumed tax rate.

Assume a villa’s account begins the month with an available cash balance of IDR 12,000,000. During the month, the owner transfers IDR 25,000,000 to fund repairs. The villa receives a net booking payout of IDR 48,000,000. It pays documented operating costs of IDR 31,500,000, including suppliers and routine operating bills, and pays IDR 8,000,000 to an owner who previously paid a documented villa invoice personally.

The cash arithmetic is:

  • Opening cash: IDR 12,000,000
  • Owner contribution: + IDR 25,000,000
  • Booking payout: + IDR 48,000,000
  • Operating payments: − IDR 31,500,000
  • Owner reimbursement: − IDR 8,000,000
  • Closing cash: IDR 12,000,000 + IDR 25,000,000 + IDR 48,000,000 − IDR 31,500,000 − IDR 8,000,000 = IDR 45,500,000

The owner contribution is not part of the IDR 48,000,000 booking payout. The reimbursement is not a second operating expense if the original invoice and payable were already recorded. The operating cash movement before owner funding is IDR 48,000,000 − IDR 31,500,000 − IDR 8,000,000 = IDR 8,500,000. The cash increase of IDR 33,500,000 also includes the IDR 25,000,000 contribution: IDR 8,500,000 + IDR 25,000,000 = IDR 33,500,000, which agrees with IDR 45,500,000 closing cash less IDR 12,000,000 opening cash.

If the owner contribution had been posted as rental income, reported revenue would be overstated by IDR 25,000,000. If the reimbursement were posted again as an expense without clearing the owner payable, costs would be overstated by IDR 8,000,000. These errors affect management decisions even before any adviser considers regulatory treatment.

What owners get wrong

1. Treating every incoming transfer as rental income

Correction: Trace the payer and purpose before posting. Owner funds, security deposits, transfers between accounts and booking payouts need separate descriptions and supporting records. A bank receipt is evidence of cash movement, not by itself evidence of revenue.

2. Recording the same owner-paid invoice twice

Correction: Record the supplier cost once, then record the amount owed to the owner or funding account. When the business pays the owner, clear that balance. Keep the invoice, payment proof and reimbursement approval together.

3. Leaving unclear balances in an unnamed “owner account”

Correction: Use a transaction log with owner name, property, purpose, date, amount, expected settlement and document status. Review old balances monthly. Ask the responsible adviser whether an unresolved amount should be treated as capital, a loan, an advance, a withdrawal or another category.

Reporting that makes the distinction useful

A monthly owner pack should not show only a bank balance. It should connect four views: operating performance, cash movement, owner funding and unresolved items.

  • Operating view: booking income, platform or management deductions, direct operating costs and other property activity.
  • Cash view: opening cash, receipts, payments, transfers, owner reimbursements and closing bank balances.
  • Funding view: owner contributions, owner-paid bills, reimbursements, withdrawals and balances by owner or property.
  • Evidence view: missing invoices, unmatched payouts, unclear transfers and items awaiting adviser or management confirmation.

Where a manager prepares the operational statement, the bookkeeper should still be able to trace its figures to source records. Differences between a management statement and the accounting file should be listed and explained, not silently forced to agree. This is especially important where the manager holds guest funds, deducts fees or pays suppliers before remitting cash.

Owners who need a repeatable monthly process can use the Bali villa monthly bookkeeping checklist alongside a dedicated owner-funding schedule.

Printable owner-contribution checklist

Use this checklist at each monthly close. Mark each item complete, attach the evidence or record why it remains open.

  1. Download all bank statements for the villa, company and relevant payment accounts.
  2. List every incoming transaction and label it as booking payout, owner funding, transfer, refund, deposit or review item.
  3. Match booking payouts to platform or direct-booking reports and investigate unmatched receipts.
  4. Collect supplier invoices, receipts, payment approvals and evidence of services received.
  5. List owner-paid expenses separately from business-account expenses.
  6. Record each owner contribution with owner, property, purpose, date, amount and supporting proof.
  7. Record each owner reimbursement only after matching it to an approved payable or claim.
  8. Check that an owner transfer has not also been posted as rental income or an expense.
  9. Allocate shared funding or costs across properties using a documented, consistently applied method.
  10. Reconcile each owner balance from opening balance through additions, settlements and closing balance.
  11. Prepare a missing-document and unresolved-classification list for management or the authorised adviser.
  12. Archive the close pack with bank reconciliations, reports, schedules and explanations.

Practical control: require a short purpose note for every owner transfer before the month is closed. If the purpose changes later, retain the original note and document the correction. That small control is more reliable than trying to reconstruct several months of ambiguous payments.

Bali Accounting provides bookkeeping support for villa and company records, including reconciliations and owner-funding schedules. Scope should be agreed separately: preparation or submission work requiring a responsible authorised person is not automatically included in a monthly bookkeeping engagement. For a Client Advisory discussion about the records your business needs, use the Client Advisory starting point.

General information disclaimer: This article is for general bookkeeping and record-keeping information only. It is not tax, legal, accounting-opinion, investment, immigration or financial advice, and it does not determine the treatment of any particular transaction. Indonesian rules and the facts of each owner, entity, property and payment arrangement can change the appropriate analysis. Obtain advice from the responsible licensed or authorised professional before relying on a classification or making a filing, submission or business decision.

Frequently asked questions

Is an owner contribution rental income?

Not automatically. It is generally tracked separately from rental income because it represents funding introduced by an owner or related party. The final classification may depend on the entity, agreements, repayment terms and applicable advice.

How should an owner-paid villa expense be recorded?

Record the documented villa expense once and track the amount owed to the owner or the relevant funding account. When the business repays the owner, clear that balance rather than recording a second expense.

Can one owner contribution fund several villas?

Yes, but the records should show how the funds were allocated. Use a documented allocation schedule identifying each property, amount, purpose and supporting payment so property-level reporting remains meaningful.

What should I do if the purpose of a transfer is unclear?

Place it in a clearly labelled review balance, collect the bank proof and surrounding documents, and ask the owner or authorised adviser to confirm its nature. Do not guess based only on the payment description.

Does separating owner funding resolve tax treatment?

No. Separation improves the evidence and bookkeeping trail, but tax treatment requires a fact-specific assessment by the responsible authorised adviser. Keep the source records and reconciliation available for that review.

title: Bookkeeping Cleanup: Building an Evidence-Based Opening Balance
contentHtml:
In bookkeeping cleanup, an opening balance should be reconstructed from dated evidence, not copied from an unexplained spreadsheet or estimated to make the trial balance agree. For a Bali villa, begin with bank statements, booking and management records, supplier documents, asset information, loans, owner funding and prior reports. Record what is supported, isolate what is uncertain, and give each unresolved item to the responsible accounting or tax adviser for a documented decision.

What an opening balance is—and why it matters

An opening balance is the amount assigned to each account at the start of the period being brought into a reliable bookkeeping system. It may include bank and cash balances, guest receivables, supplier payables, owner funding, loans, property-related assets, accumulated results and other balance-sheet accounts. It is not simply the first bank balance you can find.

For a villa, the opening position often sits across several sources. A manager may hold booking deposits, an owner may have paid suppliers personally, and a bank account may contain money belonging to more than one property. Equipment may have been purchased without an asset register. Prior reports may show a profit but no clear distinction between an owner withdrawal and an operating cost.

The objective of cleanup is therefore an evidence trail. Someone reviewing the work should be able to see the source document, the date, the amount, the account selected, the property or entity affected, the reasoning for the treatment and any remaining question. A balanced set of accounts is useful only when its figures can be explained.

Who this applies to

This guide applies to Bali villa owners, managers and companies that are changing bookkeepers, introducing accounting software, bringing several properties into one reporting system, or preparing historical records for management review. It is particularly relevant where records include cash payments, OTA payouts, management deductions, personal-card purchases, informal owner advances or several currencies.

It does not decide Indonesian tax, legal ownership, depreciation, foreign-exchange, licensing or entity questions. Those matters require the responsible authorised person. Bookkeeping preparation and any submission work are separate engagements; they are not automatically included in a monthly bookkeeping service.

Build the evidence file before posting entries

Start by defining the opening date. Do not mix a calendar-year opening with the date a new bank account was opened, the date a new manager took over or the date a company began trading. Write down the chosen date and the reason. Then create an evidence index with a reference number for every file.

  • Cash and bank: obtain statements covering the opening date, identify the account holder and currency, and note transfers between accounts.
  • Bookings and platforms: collect reservation reports, payout statements, refunds, cancellations, commissions and management statements. The reservation value is not automatically the bank receipt.
  • Supplier and operating records: gather invoices, receipts, contracts and payment confirmations for utilities, repairs, cleaning, supplies and professional services.
  • Owner activity: separate capital contributions, loans, reimbursements, private spending, withdrawals and payments made on behalf of the villa. Ask for dates and descriptions rather than relying on memory.
  • Assets and obligations: list furniture, equipment, fit-out spending, deposits, loans, unpaid bills and amounts owed to or by related parties, with supporting documents where available.
  • Prior reporting: retain earlier ledgers, trial balances, management statements and signed or approved reports. Treat them as evidence to test, not as proof that every classification is correct.

Preserve the original files. A clean-up folder should contain the source document, a working copy if needed, the proposed entry and a question log. Use consistent file names such as date, supplier, amount and reference. That simple discipline prevents a later reviewer from having to search through chat messages to understand a posting.

Use an account-by-account status

Give each proposed opening figure a status: supported, partially supported, management-confirmed, or unresolved. “Management-confirmed” means an owner has explained the transaction; it does not mean an invoice or bank record exists. An unresolved balance should remain visible in the question log instead of being hidden in revenue or miscellaneous expense.

For each item, record the source, date, currency, amount, proposed account, property, counterparty and explanation. If the evidence conflicts, retain both documents and describe the conflict. Do not overwrite an older figure simply because the newer one appears more convenient.

A practical reconstruction workflow

  1. Freeze the scope. List the entity, properties, accounts, currencies and opening date. Confirm whether the work covers bookkeeping records only or also a separate adviser review.
  2. Reconcile known cash first. Agree each bank and cash balance to a statement or count at the opening date. Explain deposits in transit, uncleared payments and transfers between accounts.
  3. Map income timing. Compare bookings, management statements, platform payouts and bank receipts. Mark stays or deposits that cross the opening date rather than forcing every amount into one period.
  4. Identify unpaid and prepaid items. Search invoices and contracts for services received but unpaid, deposits paid before service, guest deposits and other amounts that may not belong entirely to the new period.
  5. Separate owner and business movements. Trace personal payments, reimbursements, withdrawals and advances. Do not label an unexplained transfer as income merely because it increased the bank balance.
  6. Reconstruct assets and liabilities. Use purchase invoices, payment records and available agreements. If the cost or ownership cannot be supported, put it in the unresolved log and ask the responsible adviser what evidence is needed.
  7. Post proposed entries. Enter only what the evidence supports. Use a clearly identified suspense or review account only as a temporary, documented holding place—not as a permanent answer.
  8. Review the opening trial balance. Confirm that debits equal credits, then test whether each material balance has a source and an explanation. A mathematical balance is the beginning of review, not the end.

Illustrative IDR worked example: selected balances, not a complete trial balance

Assume a villa owner is reviewing records at an opening date. A bank statement supports IDR 42,000,000 in the business bank account. A supplier invoice supports a separate unpaid cleaning obligation of IDR 2,000,000. The owner also supplies evidence of a personal payment of IDR 6,500,000 for a villa repair, with a written request for reimbursement that still requires confirmation against the ledger and the agreed owner-funding arrangement. These are selected evidence items, not a complete opening balance sheet or trial balance.

For a limited cash-planning illustration only, setting aside the IDR 2,000,000 supplier payment from the stated bank balance leaves IDR 40,000,000: IDR 42,000,000 minus IDR 2,000,000. If management separately confirms and approves paying the IDR 6,500,000 owner reimbursement from that same account, the arithmetic leaves IDR 33,500,000 before all other receipts, payments, restrictions and obligations: IDR 40,000,000 minus IDR 6,500,000. This is not a measure of profit, net assets or freely distributable cash. The full ledger may contain other balances not shown here.

An additional IDR 3,000,000 owner withdrawal appears to have been included in a prior expense total. Flag it for review; do not construct a correcting journal from the bank line alone. Establish the original posting, the purpose of the withdrawal, the relevant accounting period and whether that period remains open. If an expense is still open, its reclassification must address that original expense entry; if it has already been closed into prior-period results, any opening adjustment requires a separate review of those closed balances. This example proposes no journal entry or tax treatment for that withdrawal.

The owner-funded repair needs its own evidence trail and decision about reimbursement, funding and expense or asset classification. Those decisions cannot be inferred from the selected cash-planning arithmetic. Opening equity and accumulated results must come from a supported reconstruction of the complete records, not a balancing figure invented from these few items. This is general bookkeeping information, not tax advice.

Opening-balance evidence map: illustrative only
AreaEvidence to collectControl questionStatus example
BankStatement at opening dateDoes the ledger equal the statement?Supported
Owner paymentReceipt, bank proof and explanationWas it business spending, a loan or capital?Management-confirmed
Supplier payableInvoice and service dateWas the service received before opening?Partially supported
EquipmentInvoice, payment and locationCan the item and cost be identified?Supported
Platform payoutReservation and payout reportDo booking, deductions and receipt reconcile?Unresolved

What owners get wrong

1. “If the trial balance agrees, the opening balance is correct.”

Correction: balancing only proves that the debit and credit sides are equal. It does not prove that a personal transfer was not recorded as revenue, that a payable was not omitted, or that an asset belongs to the entity. Require a source and explanation for each material balance.

2. “The previous accountant’s closing balance can be imported without review.”

Correction: use the prior records as a starting point, then test them against current bank statements, contracts, invoices and owner explanations. Carry forward a clear balance with its evidence. Flag unsupported balances rather than giving them a new account name and treating them as resolved.

3. “Every unexplained difference should go to expenses.”

Correction: an unexplained difference may represent owner funding, a loan, a transfer, a timing issue, a missing asset, a receivable or an error in another account. Put it in the review log, identify possible alternatives and obtain a documented decision from the responsible adviser or authorised management.

Printable opening-balance checklist

Print or copy this list into the cleanup workpaper. Tick each item only when the evidence and explanation have been reviewed.

  1. Define the entity, property, currency and opening date.
  2. Save statements for every bank and cash account around the opening date.
  3. List all booking channels, managers and direct-payment arrangements.
  4. Collect booking, payout, refund and management reports.
  5. Match known bank receipts to payout or transfer evidence.
  6. List unpaid supplier invoices and confirm the service period.
  7. List deposits, advances and amounts received before the service date.
  8. Separate owner contributions, loans, reimbursements and withdrawals.
  9. Inventory material furniture, equipment and fit-out items.
  10. Gather agreements and payment records for loans or related parties.
  11. Assign every proposed balance a source reference and status.
  12. Maintain a missing-document and unresolved-question log.
  13. Review foreign-currency amounts and the exchange-rate basis with an adviser where relevant.
  14. Post supported entries and label temporary review balances clearly.
  15. Reconcile the trial balance and independently review unusual movements.
  16. Prepare a handover pack containing the ledger, index, reconciliations and open questions.

Owners who need structured assistance can review Bali villa bookkeeping cleanup. A cleanup engagement should specify the periods, accounts, deliverables, evidence responsibilities and whether any authorised tax or submission work is separately included. For broader context, compare the process with cleaning up two years of messy villa books, building a practical villa chart of accounts and documenting PT PMA owner funding.

If the evidence pack has material gaps, a Client Advisory conversation can help define the bookkeeping scope and the questions that should be referred to the responsible authorised person. This is not an automatic inclusion in monthly bookkeeping, and preparation or submission work requires a separate engagement.

General information disclaimer: This article is general bookkeeping information, not tax, legal, accounting-opinion, immigration or financial advice. It does not state current tax rates, filing deadlines, penalties, thresholds or permissions. Have an appropriately licensed or authorised adviser assess your facts before relying on a classification or making a submission.

Frequently asked questions

Should I use the bank balance as my only opening balance?

No. The bank balance is one opening account. You should also investigate receivables, payables, owner activity, assets, loans, deposits and timing differences so the full financial position is supported.

What if an owner cannot find an old invoice?

Record the missing document, preserve alternative evidence such as bank proof or supplier correspondence, and label the balance as partially supported or unresolved. Do not invent an invoice or silently classify the amount as an expense.

Can a bookkeeping cleanup decide whether an owner payment is capital or a loan?

Bookkeeping can organise the evidence and present the alternatives. The owner, entity records and responsible adviser must determine the appropriate treatment based on the governing documents and facts.

How should several Bali villas share one opening balance?

Do not allocate a shared amount without a documented basis. Identify the paying entity, property benefit, date and source, then use an agreed allocation method and retain the calculation for review.

Is an unresolved balance acceptable at the end of cleanup?

It can be, if it is clearly identified, supported by a question log, assigned to someone for resolution and not misrepresented as a confirmed result. The handover should state what remains open and why.
